utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning to the technical booth, the interpreters. You may be seated. And also good morning to members of the registrar. Ms. Susan Somers, may we have the appearances, please? I see that you are the same, but I see some changes in Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, Susan Somers for the Prosecution. Also on our team is Mr. Kapila Waidyaratne, Ms. Denise Gustin, and Mr. Daniel Saxon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Defence counsel, please. Mr. Krstan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Krstan Simic. I'm representing Kvocka. Mr. Lukic today is absent because he is interviewing witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He's not here.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, he's not here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Nikolic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. The Defence counsel for the accused Kos consists of Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan, Mr. Zarko Nikolic, myself, and also we have Ms. Ristislava Mirkovic, who is here to assist communication between me and Mr. O'Sullivan, and we have permission of the registry for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I don't see Mr. Fila. Mr. Jovanovic only appears to be present.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Exceptionally today, Zoran Jovanovic will be representing the accused Mladjo Radic and Mr. Fila will be arriving tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good morning. With me is my legal assistant, Ms. Mitrovic. And co-counsel, Miodrag Deretic is working with witnesses in Prijedor, but he will be joining us on Monday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jovanovic -- no, sorry. Mr. Jovan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Myself, Jovan Simic, is representing Mr. Prcac. My co-counsel will be joining us during this week. Mr. Masic will be joining us later this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you all. We are here today to continue our work in preparation of the Defence case. At the last Status Conference we went through the items which the Defence counsel had to raise. We had a discussion with the Prosecution. The Chamber gave certain instructions to see whether it would be possible to reconsider and review our organisation of work and the presentation of Defence evidence. And the Chamber now suggests that we take stock of the situation on each point. So if we come to an agreement on certain points, that would be fine, and we will also register those we do not agree on. So I propose to give the floor to each Defence counsel, who is going to brief us on each point that was raised at the last Status Conference to see how we stand; after that we will hear the position of the Prosecution to confirm or deny whether agreement has been reached; and after that the Chamber will make its rulings. So, I shall now give the floor to Mr. Krstan Simic for him to brief us on the progress made on all these matters. Those questions were, I think, protection of witnesses, and the point was that we needed to specify each witness and each protective measure that we need so that we can make a decision. Also, there was the question of calling Witness AK, then also questions connected to the admission of exhibits. Those are the points that I remember. Maybe you have others. But in any event, I give you the floor, Mr. Krstan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Those are precisely the questions that we raised, and I think that we're making good progress. A list of witnesses has been submitted. We intend to attach the timetable of their arrivals and appearances. If any corrections, they will be reduced to a minimum, and we expect the arrival of the first seven witnesses today. Our assessment is that we need two witnesses per day, and since we will be working from the 22nd till the 25th, we feel that we will manage to fit that in. Also, we need to plan for the opening statements, and we have done our best to make sure that people don't spend too much waiting here and that we will, in the time we have at our disposal, manage to cover these witnesses. Then comes the question of Witness AK. We did not manage to come to an agreement with the Prosecution, and I called for fair play. At one point when Amir Zakic was discussed, I accepted exceptional circumstances and agreed with the Prosecution that they may use him for proving guilt. Unfortunately, we have not come to an agreement on this point, and we expect the Trial Chamber to make a ruling. In the interests of justice, it would be useful for AK to appear. He will not spend long in the courtroom, he just needs to explain certain details linked to his statement which we did not question him about, but his statement had been announced as an exhibit. And as a result, we were misled. We thought that statement would be admitted into evidence, and we thought that Your Honours would be able to take them into account in the decision-making process. We have also adjusted affidavits to the rules that were in force at the time. We had no depositions, and we also had no request for videolink testimony. Unless the Trial Chamber were to decide that individual witnesses from the affidavit lists need to be cross-examined, then for the sake of economy and for other reasons, we would resort to videolink as this would be far more favourable for the Trial Chamber than bringing those people here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel slow down, please. The interpreters are not able to follow the speed. Could counsel repeat his last sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you finished? The French interpreter tells me that the English interpreters are asking you to repeat the last sentence because they were not able to follow you.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have analysed my list of affidavits, and they appear to be absolutely acceptable according to the new Rule 92 bis, so this should not cause any problems, and we expect that question to be raised during the discussion today, later on at this hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There may be some problems here because you mentioned the 22nd to the 25th, but I think we need to say from the 22nd to the 26th because the week is 22 to the 26th. That is the whole week.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, from the beginning of the plan we have the dates 22nd to the 25th, and we were confused by this change because all the timetables that all Defence counsel have, have the time period for hearings indicated as 22 to the 25th. So four days now, from the 5th to the 9th, another four, plus five, makes it a total of 13 days. Those were our calculations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There may indeed be some confusion because from the beginning the Chamber had intended to sit for the whole week. There's no reason why we should not sit on Friday, but if this causes a problem in terms of organisation, fine. However, if there is a possibility to sit on Friday, it is always important to take advantage of the time available. I don't know where this confusion came from because from the beginning we said that we would be working all week. When we talk about a week, it means Monday through Friday. But if that is a problem for you, Mr. Krstan Simic, we will accept 22nd till the 25th, but it is a shame. I don't know who is at fault and where the source of the problem lies, but never mind. So I'll give the floor now to Ms. Susan Somers for her comments, if she has any reaction to what Mr. Krstan Simic has just said.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I first indicate that it is no problem for the Prosecution to work on the 26th. We welcome the extra day if it works out for the Defence. On the issue of the affidavit, under the -- the former B known as affidavit for Mr. Kvocka, in the 65 ter submission of Mr. Simic, there was no summary as required for the affidavit witnesses. There may perhaps have been some confusion, although it appears -- there's no doubt in our mind that those are witness summaries, albeit proposed in non-live form, and must be included in the 65 ter submission. They are not, and we do not know the content of the affidavits. We would otherwise have tried to make the same assessment about cross-examination or not had we had them. So we would ask, and we did ask yesterday at a conference which Mr. Simic and everyone attended, to try to get to us immediately the affidavits so that we can indicate to the Chamber and to Defence counsel what we think would be, in our judgement, appropriate for cross-examination, or just let it go in. I also wanted to point out on behalf of my colleagues as well who asked me to raise this, there was a bilateral concern about our sitting on the cusp of a change in the rules, and we will ask, of course, for guidance from the Court as to whether the spirit of 94 ter will persist, or if we will go into immediately the strict terms of 92 bis. On the issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Do you have a position on that, Ms. Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, looking at Rule 6 and the position -- the language that is insistent on no prejudice being worked, in effect, because the Defence has prepared its case based on the old rule, I think if the Court were to consider that those guidelines were -- at least, those affidavits which were dated prior to, if we had to have a cutoff point, we would not object. I think it is not critical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You would not object to what, to their coming in under the old rule?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Well, in terms of -- we have the same rights to object and say that, no, it's not appropriate and we want to cross; but in terms of any matters of form or -- of course, under the old rule, it was very strict by corroborating --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right, right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: -- whereas it seems to be, depending on how one reads it, and there's been not much interpretation in the three days or whatever --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: It just came into being today.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, I know, Your Honour, and therefore we're not sure how it will be interpreted. But we leave it in the Chamber's hands. We want fairness on this to be the guidance since we all have worked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But want to I point out to you that Rule 6(D) is, "An amendment shall enter into force in seven days, but shall not operate to prejudice the rights of the accused." It doesn't say anything about Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm painfully aware --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I understand you may have a different interpretation, but I only point out it would be the -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In fact, Your Honour, we were speaking exactly of its provisions. We had discussed this yesterday, and there was voiced a great deal of concern, and we wanted the Chamber to be aware of this right off the bat. So we are in the Chamber's hands, again, as long as -- even if it's not voiced in the rule, I know this Chamber has always been cognizant of the fairness to the Prosecution [Realtime transcript read in error "fairness as well"] as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: On the issue -- excuse me one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. There is a word missing. You said "cognizant of the fairness to the Prosecution."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Always. It's always been fair, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Because here it is missing. They don't say it to the Prosecution, so let them add it to prove that we are fair to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Absolutely. And I apologise. I'm told I'm speaking too fast, and I will slow down. Thank you, Your Honour, for catching that. On the issue of Witness AK, a couple of points, if I may. One is that although the Prosecution -- AK was designated Prosecution witness, and I don't believe that that designation leaves the witness, particularly in light of the fact that as a -- there is a standing agreement or there is a standing protective order that indicates that contact with Prosecution witnesses - and it does not limit the phase of the trial - should be at least done with notice to or through the Prosecution. This was not done. We were unaware of contact by the Defence with AK, which causes us some concern. Secondly, I see no fair play issue. The Zjakic situation was a witness who would have come but for the physical condition. And I've read the transcripts, Your Honour. It appears the Bench was fully cognizant of the situation and assisted us in allowing this witness nonetheless to give evidence for the case in chief, albeit at the time of rebuttal, but not part of the rebuttal case. This has been done in other Chambers. It is a practice that I think is well accepted. That is a witness who has never shown. AK is a witness who was here, and having reviewed the transcript, it appears, from the representations by my counsel opposite, that the areas of inquiry for AK at the time of being called for the Defence would be the same areas that would have been very much the proper subject of cross. It was a fairly broad direct and in fact would have cried out for such questions. And I think it becomes a matter for the Court to determine whether we want to go down the road of calling back witnesses when the Rule, Rule 90, obligates the entire case to be put at the time. The witness may or may not be willing. I don't think that's the principal issue here. I think it's an issue of what the Rules require and whether or not there's compliance with the Rules. On the -- I think as to this particular accused, that's pretty much what we discussed. We -- I would like to represent to the Chamber that all of us, all counsel who were present yesterday, agreed that as between depositions, which they know we are not terribly in favour of, and videolink, if there is going to be some action in Banja Luka, that videolink is okay with all parties. And as we will progress through this hearing, the Chamber will realise that we have, at least as to one accused, we've examined everything that we have, but we've cut back on objections on three or four, so it would limit -- and of course, we're only asking for cross on certain affidavits, and we're trying to cut down the amount of time that the Chamber would actually have to be engaged with this so that we can persuade the Chamber that it would be a preferable method to the deposition method. But again there is agreement. There's no objection by any of counsel to the use of videolink. I do want to indicate to the Chamber that I have made inquiry of our office, and I know that this is a registry function, but just to make sure that there was no particular procedural problem for scheduling and that the Banja Luka facility of -- is available for such -- is available, is up and running for such type of conference, and the room is quite appropriate, from my observation. I think for this particular point -- I'll just check with my colleague, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krstan Simic, have you any additional questions to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall be very brief. I have two comments to make. There is no dispute over the fact that I have contacted Witness AK, because I understood the instructions that one could not contact the witness until the end of his testimony, because after all, the trial can go on for five or six years and this would put us in an absurd position, and that would border on human rights. Another far more important question is the following: In this case the Prosecution has appropriated certain witnesses, and your Chamber, on one occasion, said that witnesses were witnesses of the truth and justice. Judge Hunt also repeated the other day that these were witnesses of events and not the property of the Prosecution. And I really think that in a fair trial, there should be no obstacle to counsel contacting Prosecution witnesses if they so wish, because this is in the interest of the efficiency of the proceedings and in the interest of justice. I consider this to be an exception, and surely this will not be repeated often. This is the first time that we are asking for anything like this. The witness is willing to come. The Defence feel that there is reason for him to come. This witness testified in an impressive manner in Court. Why not give him another chance to contribute to justice? The question of affidavits, again we differed. In my view, in accordance with Rule 65, the Defence is not obliged to produce summaries of affidavits. This is not provided for. These are special statements that the Defence may use in support or to corroborate the statement of certain witnesses. All the affidavits have been prepared. You have two available today that have been disclosed seven days prior to the calling of the witness, in accordance with the Rules, and the Prosecution has already received them, Rule 94 ter. And then within seven days we will address the counsel -- the Chamber to see what should be done next. We feel there is no need to provide affidavits earlier on unless we are given explicit orders. Therefore, all the affidavits will be translated on Monday and they will be tendered in accordance with Rule 94 ter if we decide to apply that Rule in the course of these proceedings. If the Trial Chamber feels it is more useful to expedite proceedings, I can hand them over to Ms. Somers as soon as they are translated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Krstan Simic. Thank you very much. Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Just one or two points, Your Honour. One is that apparently other counsel have understood that it is necessary still to go through the Prosecution, as we appreciate Mr. Jovan Simic asked us to contact four witnesses at the last session, which we did. We've reported back to these witnesses -- to Mr. Simic that three or four have indicated they are not willing and one is. I think that there's no basis for the position that Mr. Krstan Simic is taking. And further, my recollection of the transcript is that certain witnesses, AG and AH, were described very firmly as Kvocka witnesses. So there is some -- I think it's going to be a point of concern. We ask only that we be given a chance to approach the witness first and that we know that the witness has been approached. After all, it is very possible that a witness who was a Prosecution witness may come back on rebuttal. And in fact, the designation stays as do protections. They are not lifted. They persist. The point made about the affidavits -- and I'll try not to beat a dead horse. However, if this -- if the position that Mr. Simic is taking were correct, then there could be an unlimited constant addition of new witnesses, and that's not the purpose of 65 ter. It is to give, to the best degree possible at the time of the commencement of trial, a definitive witness list. It doesn't matter the form. It just says in 65 ter a list of witnesses, and affidavit witnesses are a form. And therefore we would ask the Chamber to simply look at the plain language of the Rule, in the same way that 94 bis experts we don't have to provide at the time of the 65 ter the actual statement. That is governed by another Rule. However, we must inform of the use, and it's consistent with the use of 94 bis that anything for affidavits would also be included so that we would at least be on notice of the nature of the testimony, and I think it would help us speed up some of the inquiries the Chamber would like us to make. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I've just got a question. I want to make sure I understand what you think is necessary under the old 94 ter. If the party submits to you an affidavit in advance -- it doesn't say how much in advance; it just says filed prior to the giving of testimony by the witness. Okay. So they give you the affidavit and they say, "This affidavit is submitted in corroboration of Witness X, who is going to testify next Monday," and the points on which it's allegedly corroborating are A, B, and C, why do you have to have anything other than that under the Rule?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We don't have that, actually. We don't have a designation of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: What don't you have? You have the affidavits --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: From this particular accused, no, Your Honour we don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But you will -- he has to give them to you in advance of the testimony of the live witness that they're supposed to be connected with.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The practice, as I have seen it in other Chambers, is that they are listed as witnesses. The more specific information is given, the actual affidavit is given up front so that we can make an objection and that we can ask, if appropriate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: It has to be given under Rule 94 ter. It has to -- it doesn't say how long, but it says it has to be given in advance of the testimony. That might be up to the Chambers to say how long. I --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I think the appellate decision, Your Honour -- excuse me if I cut you off on that last word. The appellate decision, I believe, from Kordic discusses the timing on affidavits, because the exclusion that resulted there was a failure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But that was after.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It was. In reading the Rules, it appears, though, that we should at least have enough of a summary at the time of the 65 ter submission to know the guts of what the affidavit witness will say. The actual affidavit should be presented so that we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So that you have it before the live witness to whom it's connected.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Exactly. Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But I gather your complaint at this stage is not that you won't get the affidavit before the live witness appears - you would have to do that or it would be in violation of the Rule completely - but that you don't get a summary of what's in the affidavit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Correct. Under 65 ter, because they are in fact witnesses again, as a 94 bis witness is a witness to be listed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Has that about been the practice in other Chambers? We haven't had it come up here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It has in Kordic, Your Honour. All the witnesses -- our experts were listed with just a summary, minor summary, and then of course within the provisions of the Rule, we filed timely. I cannot address any other Chamber, but certainly that was a Chamber of very active litigation, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, I have your interpretation, although I note 65 ter G is a list of witnesses the Defence intends to call. I don't know. I guess that could be interpreted either way.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I think so. The practice has been, at least as we have done it, to consider them witnesses, and I think that that's a fair interpretation which puts everyone on notice. It speeds things up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps to make an observation, one must bear in mind that when you speak the same -- as you speak the same language, you must bear in mind that we are working through interpreters and I think the French interpreter was struggling in following you. I think that we now have raised some issues that the Chamber will be deliberating. We are not going to give you a ruling now, but we are going to take into consideration everything that has been said so far. I should nonetheless like to make a comment with respect to what Mr. Krstan Simic was saying with respect to the witnesses and their relationship to the Tribunal. I continue to feel, but maybe that is my own personal opinion, perhaps I'm not speaking in the name of the Chamber, the witnesses are presented by the parties. But they are witnesses of justice, and I don't think that any of the party can appropriate a witness, in my view. And once the witness has testified in court, his testimony, if I can say so and put this in inverted commas, "property"; he is the property of justice. His testimony is not the property of anybody. Testimony is given under oath here in the courtroom. Perhaps this is a deception which stems from our different cultures. We have different systems, different cultures, different ways of conceiving witnesses. I personally, as I have said, and I would like to stress, this it is my own personal opinion, I believe that witnesses do not belong to anybody. They belong to themselves, and therefore are always in the function of justice. But we shall be taking into account everything that has been said on these issues, and let us move on now to Mr. Nikolic, that is to say, the Kos Defence team. I see that Mr. O'Sullivan is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'd like to concur with what the president has said. It's not his personal opinion, and I think it is the Bench's, with the permission of Judge Wald that we are all here, without distinction between Prosecution, Defence, and the Bench. We are here for international justice. So the case is not the case of the Prosecution or the Defence. It is our own mission, all of us, to contribute to establish justice with regard to war crimes and human rights. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you to Judge Riad, and I give the floor to Mr. O'Sullivan. I think the issues that we have with respect to the Kos trial, if I remember correctly, were as follows -- would you like to remind me, please, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you and good morning. There are a few matters I'd like to raise in light of our last conference and also in light of the meeting we had yesterday with the Prosecution. One matter that is still open is the timing of the opening statements by the Defence. Kos's position is that we should make our opening statements prior to our Defence beginning. As for matters that arose yesterday in the meeting with the Prosecution, there are four points. First, the Prosecution is a gracious host and they served good coffee, and we thank them for that. And the second point doesn't directly affect Kos because Kos has no affidavits, but it does affect the conduct of the case, and I think the parties will need guidance from the Chamber on whether or not we follow 94 -- or 92 bis or 94 ter. And our position is that will affect the latter two points, and they are, first - and I believe I'm giving the correct position agreed upon by all the parties - is that our preference is videolink over deposition from Banja Luka. And in the event of cross-examination of affidavits, that would also be done by videolink from Banja Luka. And the final point on videolink is that we may in fact require five videolinks, videolinks at five different times, one per case, one for each defendant. It may arise that through a combination of deposition evidence and cross-examination of affidavits, there may in fact be a need to have that occur during each of the five Defence cases. I believe that reflects the agreement that the parties wish to present to the Chamber. And the third point which is of a concern to us in the management of this case arises in light of what appears to be a break in the Krstic case and the timing and scheduling of our trial. And the important point there for the Defence is to ensure that if we are going to work more than previously foreseen, that there be a break between the cases nonetheless so that there can be a week or so or a reasonable period for the upcoming case, that is, that counsel can make sure everything is in place to run that defendant's case smoothly. So those are the points, Your Honour, which Kos wishes to discuss this morning, and we request Your Honours' guidance and determination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Do you have a position, Mr. O'Sullivan, or one preferably on behalf of all counsel, as to whether or not you think we should follow 94 ter hence forth or 92 bis, especially in light of the line I quoted from Rule 6 that talks about especially worrying about prejudice to the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't think I should speak to that because it's -- since we don't have affidavits, I haven't addressed my mind to the impact of how that might affect the other parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there's really nothing that we can add. Mr. O'Sullivan and the Prosecution did speak of this, and we thank him for representing the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. Mr. Jovanovic is next.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. At yesterday's meeting with the Prosecution, the Defence of the accused Mladjo Radic handed over to the Prosecution a set of expert findings and witness statements and affidavits, signed statements; and we mentioned which of those affidavits or witness statements are being translated currently, and this was done following a previous agreement; and with our desire to hear from the Prosecution, in which cases they would be calling for cross-examination. It is the position of the Defence of Mr. Mladjo Radic as regards expert findings that we hand in a written report, and that that should take the place of the presentation in chief. After the Prosecution has studied those findings, I can only suppose that they will say in which cases they will be calling for a cross-examination. And the same applies to witnesses and the testimonies that were taken following Rule 94 ter, on the basis of Rule 94 ter: It is the position of the Defence of the accused Radic is that if possible and if the Chamber agrees, that we continue working along the lines of Rule 94 ter. The Prosecution also intimated, in view of the witnesses from whom statements have been taken in that way, that they were witnesses which the Prosecution will certainly insist upon having a cross-examination. If the Chamber agrees to this request by the Prosecution, the Radic Defence feels that this could be done by means of videolink. So we have reached full agreement on that point. If the Trial Chamber decides to establish a videolink connection for the examination of witnesses whose statements were taken on the basis of Rule 94 ter, the Radic Defence would like to propose for practical purposes that the -- that most of the witnesses that have been put forward for testimony before the Trial Chamber, that they, too, be heard via videolink in Banja Luka. That would mean that out of the 26 witnesses, of the 26 witnesses mentioned in the motion regarding 94 ter, that is to say, the majority of the witnesses would be heard in Banja Luka. And the Prosecution, that is to say, Ms. Somers, mentioned that technical facilities are being prepared and that there is a location where this could be done. The facilities exist. And so most of the witnesses would be heard there. If we follow Rule 92 bis, and in view of the contents of the statements, witness statements, that is to say, the affidavits, then those witnesses would be heard by means of videolink. Both the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination would be held by videolink. Of course, this will affect time, the time that has been asked for, for the presentation of evidence of the accused Radic. And if this -- if we were to have most of the proceedings conducted by videolink, the presentation of evidence and testimony of witnesses before the Chamber, the Radic Defence case would need two days -- it would need two weeks for the videolink, and if the Prosecution so requires, then time for the cross-examination as well. The second issue that we discussed last time was the question of medical documentation, but I think that we could discuss that matter in a closed session, so we can perhaps leave that issue to later on. We need not go into it at this point. I should just like to mention is that we have the same expert findings, the affidavits and the witness statements are ready for trial, and I shall be handing them in to the registrar in the course of the day. Of course, we also know that before the trial, we should send in those statements. Again, this was just by way of informing the Prosecution and the Court, and our wish is to hear the position of the Prosecution with respect to the affidavits and where they seek cross-examination as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Jovanovic. Ms. Susan Somers, there is a matter that we shall be discussing perhaps later on in private session, but for the moment, would you like to respond to the issues raised by Mr. Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Just one point I need to make - excuse me - absolutely clear is that the videolink has not yet been prepared. That is a registry function, and so as long as counsel understands that we've simply made the inquiry about the appropriateness of the facility, and we were informed that it was. And once the Chamber authorises the manner, then the registry would have to do what it has to do. I think there really wasn't any other matter other than the referral -- the reference to the private session, I think. Oh, excuse me, may I just tell the Court one point. It is true we were handed, and we do appreciate, a very thick volume of materials last night which we are trying to wade through, and at the very earliest, perhaps even -- if the Chamber might grant us time before the commencement of testimony, we can announce some of the issues on acceptance or requests for cross-examination of the affidavit issues. We'll try to do it over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers, with respect to the reports, expert reports, I have a question to ask you. You said that in principle, you are going to object to the admission of these reports, and if that is so, then you would like to cross-examine the experts. Is it possible for you to respond in writing to those reports? Can you respond to them in writing and so avoid calling back the experts?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: My --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but let me just tell you that in another case this is what we did, and I think the results were good. A party was not in agreement with the findings of an expert witness, and the other party found a counter-report, expert report. So my question is, do you have the possibility of finding a response in writing, of finding an expert to come up with a written response to the first expert report?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think much of it would depend on the subject matter of the expert report. I am very willing to explore possible remedy or possible resolution on certain types of experts. There may be some matters, and for example, I can think of one proposed report, we've certainly not seen it, but the summary suggests that we would probably file a motion to exclude it altogether on relevance. So if the Chamber agrees, there may be one report less with which to deal. There is some subject matter that I think is -- may not lend itself well to that type of response, but where appropriate, if the Chamber will allow me, once I see the report, I would certainly consider that option, and I would -- the sooner I have the report, the sooner I can get a counter-expert, as it were, or an expert to assist us in our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At all events, Ms. Somers, as you know, there is at least one report presented by the Defence as a response to another report already tendered by the Defence, by the Prosecution I think to the registry. So as regards the other expert reports, perhaps the Prosecution can respond in like manner. But I do understand your position: After having read the reports, you will be able to state your position. So I thank you for your attention. Let us now move on to the Defence counsel again, and it is the Defence team of Mr. Zigic, counsel Stojanovic has the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I shall be brief and just speak about affidavits. So far we have not had a single affidavit, but we have accepted your proposals that this would be a good way of presenting certain evidence and ones that we were to have presented by deposition. In the meantime, the rules have been amended, and I think the question is rather complicated, that is to say, how far we could apply Rule 6 (d) to our particular case. For the moment let me say we are studying the new Rule, that is 92 bis, Rule 92 bis, and we feel that Rule 92 bis provides a rather different framework with respect to affidavits, and we could try to do something with respect to that Rule and present something to the Court along the lines of that Rule. But at any rate, we do agree that a lot can be done through videolink, so videolink as a mode, as a procedure, is acceptable to us. Another problem that we highlighted was the problem of confidential contributions, and I don't think that at yesterday's meeting we were able to come to an agreement with our colleagues from the Prosecution on that issue. So far in the course of preparing our Defence case, we interviewed superficially some potential witnesses, bearing in mind the confidentiality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stojanovic, I see Ms. Somers on her feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption to the bench and to counsel. If this is the discussion that I believe it will become, it would be appropriate for a brief private session, and I have what I think might be some good news for Mr. Stojanovic and counsel. We met again as a team afterward and tried to come to some solution that may be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stojanovic, perhaps you could leave that matter regarding confidentiality to a private session, and then we could take the two issues together, the issue raised by the Radic Defence and your one. Do you agree, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do agree, Your Honours. Perhaps the next issue, however, would be conducive to a private session as well. It is the use of Witness R's transcript, and he was a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And all that remains for me now in open session to mention an incident which I have already told the Prosecution about, but they suggested that I should put it to the Trial Chamber. The day before yesterday in Belgrade a courier --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see Ms. Somers, Madam Somers on her feet again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: My apologies again. I wanted to make it clear to the Chamber that when this was raised to me, I suggested it perhaps be a private session matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stojanovic, do you agree to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you have completed everything you wish to say in open session. Thank you. We just have the question of affidavits and the new rule or sworn statements. I don't know if Ms. Somers would like to add anything on that point before we go into private session to discuss the remaining issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Krstan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need to give an answer whether we are with a new or old rule. I prefer sticking to 94 ter, Rule 94 ter. So as not to come into a position where this issue should be raised again, I think that Rule 6 implies that after the Prosecution concludes, we can continue with the Rule on the basis of the previous Rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So Ms. Somers, her response to some questions raised by Mr. Stojanovic. We have not yet heard the position of the Prcac Defence team. So, has Ms. Somers got anything to add to questions raised by the Zigic Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. They will all be reserved for the private session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Jovan Simic, what issues do you have to raise with respect to the Prcac Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, we don't have any major problems yet, and happily, we are dealing with all the outstanding issues between ourselves and the Prosecution outside the courtroom. But the Prcac Defence would like to insist that the previous Rule 94 ter be applicable because otherwise, this would change the entire concept of our Defence, and we would need additional time. You know that time has been an issue right from the start. So that our Defence has been conceived on the basis of affidavits, and if we were to go by the new rules, this would be a considerable problem to us, especially as the 92 bis rule is quite different to what the previous 94 ter rule states. And as we have Rule 6(D) as well, I think that we should proceed along those lines. And yesterday at the meeting I think we had reached a consensus with respect to -- that is to say, we aligned our views, the Defence teams and the Prosecution, with respect to videolinks because then we would be able to marry the two, and this would reduce the amount of time needed and the costs incurred. As far as all the other issues are concerned, I support Mr. O'Sullivan. I do believe that pauses are needed between the different Defence team presentations because, for example, in the course of a week, one Defence team could complete its case and then the other to begin on Thursday, for example. Logistically speaking, technically speaking, this would be a problem, not because the Defence teams are not ready, but I would ask the Trial Chamber to take this into consideration. As far as the Prcac Defence is concerned we just have one more issue. We have contacted the Prosecution with respect to having contact with certain witnesses, and we're told by them that we could contact one of the Prosecution witnesses. We can go ahead with that, and we shall do so and inform you of that in due course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jovan Simic, is there any news with respect to a matter you raised, exhibits to be examined by the Prosecutor in order to know whether the Prosecution is contesting their authenticity or not? Do you remember the issue I mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prcac Defence has handed over all the exhibits. There was a slight misunderstanding with respect to the list of witnesses and list of witnesses who have given affidavits, but I think we have put that misunderstanding right and it is now up to the Prosecution, because we have supplied them with all the written evidence, certifications and certificates, and so on. So the Defence has tendered all this to the Prosecution before the deadline, and all that we have to see now is what they think about it, and we are awaiting their response. Thank you. I should like to state that this Defence team is still undergoing its investigations, and in keeping with Article 65 ter, I wrote in my submission that we retain the right to send in some new exhibits, evidence. It will not be great in bulk, nor will it refer to any crucial issues, but we do reserve that right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Simic. With regard to what you said that when a Defence team finishes its turn, do we need -- do you suggest that we should have a pause of several days before the other one starts? Is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I supported what Mr. O'Sullivan was saying on the subject; that is to say, between the end of the Defence case of one team and the start of the Defence case of another team, several days' pause in between.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And in spite of the fact you said that the Defence teams are ready? Is it because of the witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because of organisation, technical problems with respect to bringing in the witnesses. It is not a matter of Defence itself, but logistical problems, technical problems in actually bringing the witnesses to Court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But that will cause a great delay, you know. Already each part -- each accused has two weeks, so the other knows, the other team knows when to start, logistically speaking, or approximately. At worst, the witness will have to wait for a day or two, and they do all the time. Don't you think we are in need of time, to gain time, for the sake of the accused too? That's my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I quite agree that we need to save on time, and I think that this Defence team has saved quite a bit of time. But I think that the fact that we know that in April or the beginning of May this Defence counsel needs to present its case, it doesn't mean that we can prepare the witnesses in time. This involves a great deal of organisation. People are away on business, are sick. We cannot keep them waiting for 10 or 15 days somewhere and then tell them that they should get on a plane and come here. This is not just my position; it is the position of all Defence counsel, as far as I understand. We will all have difficulties there. My learned friend O'Sullivan mentioned this already and I just supported him. Also colleague Krstan Simic mentioned this. He is the first, so he will not be having that problem, but all the other Defence teams will. So we do need two or three days to go to Banja Luka or Prijedor, because even though we do have some investigators working on the ground, any changes in the plan or timetable affect the witnesses, and it's different when they communicate with the investigator or with the counsel or co-counsel. This is just my suggestion. I don't insist upon it. I just agreed and supported the suggestion of Mr. O'Sullivan. I think that if we organise ourselves well, we will save more time than if we act in the way that the Prosecution has done sometimes so that witnesses had to wait quite -- for some time. So I think this would be a better way to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to give the floor to Ms. Susan Somers, but after that I do wish to come back to this question of organisation, bearing in mind the interests of the witnesses. Ms. Susan Somers, you have the floor to respond to some matters raised by the Prcac Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Mr. Simic was extremely helpful in providing us essentially with -- we thought they were affidavit -- we thought what we were being provided with was the list of affidavit witness. In fact, for every witness there was an affidavit. So in the group of 14 with which we were provided, some are going to be live testimony, as I understand it. However, having reviewed the list that was -- the documents were which given to us, we were able to come up with - and I hope this helps the Chamber and the Defence - 8 of the 11 we would ask for cross on. So three we would have no problem with admission right out. And one we will move to strike -- we will move to exclude based on relevance; and if in fact it is admitted, we will deal with it after the Chamber's ruling. Going back to Your Honour's question about the Prosecution in this case, and I limit it to this case, but the view on 94 versus 92, there certainly is an overarching concern with fairness and expedition. And our position -- we leave it in the Chamber's hands, understanding that for us we would go along with a ruling that allows us to have summaries of the affidavits timely. 65 ter, as you will, paragraph, just so we know where we stand in terms of where the proposed witness will speak, or about which she will speak; then, in fact, have the affidavits in time to incorporate points in them if they are accepted into the cross-examination. And if -- and assuming we have enough time to present to the Chamber objections on the affidavits, if we feel that they should not be accepted in whole, or if accepted, that we would reserve cross, and then have the chance to cross-examine where we ask for that opportunity. And I think if those are the pole stars, the guidelines, I think the Chamber would be able to fashion a remedy that would take into account all interests, so that we really lose nothing that we would have had and that they are not thrown off by a long-set course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether Mr. Jovan Simic has anything to add. I don't think so. No. You gave us a sign that you have nothing to add. This question that Mr. O'Sullivan, Mr. Jovan Simic, and I think other Defence counsel have raised in terms of the organisation of Defence counsel regarding witnesses: As you know, we are always concerned about this, and I have said many times - I said it to the Prosecution - that the witness [as interpreted] prefers not to have a witness for the last half of Friday, then having a witness who would stay on to appear for an hour on Monday. So I think we should address this together with the Witness Unit so as to organise ourselves well. But I think for things to flow smoothly, it is really necessary to have a little pause, but which, in my opinion, must not be long; otherwise we will be risking delaying the end of the proceedings too much. And this is one of our prime concerns, to complete the case. And the accused have the right to have a final decision, and that is our concern. But we must try and do so in a calm manner and with serenity, without pressure, without rushing things, without stress. So perhaps we must examine how this can be achieved. And I even think, if necessary -- I'm making such an appeal. I see that all Defence counsel are not complete today, and this may be a good thing. I know they're not on holiday; they're working. So if the situation arises when we should have one Defence counsel here and another one preparing the next stage, perhaps we should do that. We don't necessarily have to have all Defence counsel present here in the courtroom. However, that does not apply to the Judges. Taking all this into consideration, I think we shall try to strike a balance so that things can proceed smoothly. I don't know whether we have other matters to address. I think we do. Mr. O'Sullivan mentioned the question of opening statements, and at the Status Conference on the 28th of November we already addressed that matter, I think, and at that Status Conference the response was that Kvocka does need three quarters of an hour, Kos one hour, Radic one hour and Prcac one hour. Can you confirm all that now regarding opening statements? I see nods. If you cannot confirm this, please tell us. So the matter is resolved. We also mentioned that the schedule of the Chamber, due to unforeseen circumstances, has slightly changed. So this is a question that affects Mr. Krstan Simic most, but the other counsel as well, whether it would be possible to sit during the week of the 29th of January to the 2nd of February. Mr. Krstan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I learnt about this possibility this morning, and in view of the problems that we have been drawing attention to constantly, that is, the problem of witnesses, we have made a plan. People have been told when they would testify, in what order, that they have to get permission to leave from their companies, and I think it would cause really enormous problems for us to change that timetable. I must tell you that it took us a lot of effort to convince the witnesses to appear here, and now if I were to call them up and tell them, "The schedule has changed. You must come on another date," I think that would be most inconvenient. I too, however, would like to complete this case as soon as possible, but I think that is unrealistic, because the witnesses have been told the dates when they are due to appear and they have adjusted their plans accordingly. So I would be placed in a most embarrassing position in relation to the witnesses. I might be able to organise myself, but I don't know about the witnesses. Then also the organisation of witness travel. I plan to bring the witnesses for a whole week, all of them. It is cheaper and simpler for one man to go and pick them up and take them back rather than bringing them one by one. People also feel afraid when they're alone. And I think this would affect the plans of the Defence and would very seriously disrupt those plans.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me suggest something else. I think it is a luxury, in my point of view, not to use the courtroom when we have so much work to do, but there are things that happen that we cannot foresee in advance. And if we look at our case -- I don't wish to pressure you, but you, as the parties, do you see any other possibility for using up this time available? Mr. Krstan Simic, do you see any other way in which we could fill up this available time?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we are the first, and we are faced with a fait accompli. So I have spoken to Mr. Simic, saying that it would be desirable that we should make a new timetable today and take into consideration the free time in the courtroom so that the people that follow me could plan their time. I am now working on the opening statements and the bringing in of witnesses. I have planned their arrival for the 3rd. Their passports are in the administration. I wish I could have a magic wand and bring them in here over night, but that is not possible. They need to get visas, to get tickets and everything. I've just been going through all of this. This is really very complicated. The bureaucracy is highly involved, and I think that would be too ambitious. We are ready, there is no doubt about it, but we have planned to continue our case until the 16th. If we go into March a little, then Mr. Kos would give us that time and by then we would be completed. But all we need is enough time to let the people know who are expected to come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Krstan Simic. Ms. Susan Somers, my question to you: Do you see a way of filling in the time? It's true that we have a lot to do, but the courtroom availability is an important issue, and I'd like to hear you before I try and convey to you my suggestions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we completely concur with the Chamber's position that every available hour in Court should be used. I don't know whether or not -- there may be sufficient time in advance. If the issue for Mr. Simic were his witnesses' travel, if he wanted -- and again, this is completely not in my hands, but I'm throwing it out. If he were interested in possibly shifting some of the testimony to a video in Banja Luka if that might be of assistance. If the registry feels there is sufficient time to set up, it would occupy the days and it would possibly make it easier for his local witnesses if they didn't have to take two days off but rather a half day; in other words, we come to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we should consult the Witness Unit to see whether this is possible, because it is the Unit that deals with witnesses and arranges for visas and everything. I don't know whether it is possible to speed up those procedures to bring the witnesses forward. Maybe it is difficult, maybe even impossible, but we should consult the Witness Unit. However, before giving you the floor, Mr. Simic, let me introduce my idea. My idea -- I know it's always difficult to change plans, but we do have the accused who wish to testify. We have the cross-examination of the other accused. And the accused are here; they're available, aren't they? So the question of the order, we can adapt to it intellectually, I think. We have decided that the cross-examination of Mr. Kvocka and Mr. Radic should be done at the end of the Defence case, but we were open. I felt both the Prosecution and the Defence to agree with beginning the cross immediately. In my opinion, it would be possible, at least to cross-examine Mr. Radic and Mr. Kvocka. It is a suggestion I'm making to you. I am not trying to pressure you. I wanted to hear your suggestions first. I hope you feel quite free to tell the Chamber what you think about this. It is a suggestion of the President of the Chamber, because I haven't spoken about it with my colleagues. So Mr. Krstan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we support such a position. I think that is a possibility for making the best of that time. So you have our agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much, Mr. Krstan Simic. Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the position of Mr. Radic's Defence was that the cross-examination should be done now, as opposed to the request of the Prosecution that it be done at the end. So we are quite ready for it. We quite agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers. So it's up to you now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I kind of hate to be the bad guy, but I have to say that it would be very difficult for us to change or to rework the order now, as we have set everything in motion geared to having all of the case in front of us, and I think that it would provide the best cross-examination if we did not deviate from that. Our position was that - and the Court, of course, factored into its decision, as I understood, from our representations last time - that we had at all times planned to go at the end of the case of the defendant. And I can represent that it would not be okay with the Prosecution to deviate from that now because of the way we have undertaken preparation. I apologise for what may be a perceived inflexibility. It really is not. It's a question of, in part, my own position having to do a bit of extra catching up and making sure that I miss nothing, and also to, more importantly, to make sure that the Bench is not left without some point that we are obligated to get in at the end of -- so that the whole case is examined. And therefore, if there were some other means by which we could use up that time -- unless, perhaps, there's flexibility on the Defences' part to do their opening statements earlier, maybe that would be an alternative that would not be terribly disruptive of any substantive examination. But for us, it would be very, very difficult, and I would ask the Court to stand by its original ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will render a decision about this, but I thought that I understood at the last Status Conference that the Prosecution was open to the possibility of beginning the cross-examination of Mr. Kvocka and Mr. Radic now. You always expressed a preference, but in any event, we will have to decide on the matter. What is our concern is that for us, but I think that I can say for the Tribunal, including the Prosecution, it is a luxury to allow a week to go by not using a courtroom, and this is of the greatest concern to us. So I don't see that there are any other matters to deal with for the Status Conference. Oh, yes, of course, we have to go into private session. Perhaps we should have a break first. I see Ms. Susan Somers and Mr. Stojanovic on their feet. Ladies first? Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. If I may ask the Chamber and counsel to indicate at what position in terms of witnesses we might find ourselves at that time, that would be helpful to see if there's any give or take that I can try to negotiate in terms of the way we've undertaken things. And I am hesitant to say anything more, but if perhaps we can get an honest estimate of where we might be at the time of that break, then I might have a chance to make it a little bit easier if I'm confident that we've had enough opportunity to do the yeoman's share of what we have set out to do in terms of preparation for examination. I do not wish to cause a problem for the Chamber, and in terms of the issue of preference, I had looked into the discussion between Mr. Fila and Mr. Niemann, and it really was pretty much left, "We appreciate the concession on going out of order, and therefore you choose the time." So I think it was pretty much at all times understood, at least by us, that we would go at the end. I apologise if there was any confusion to the Chamber. Perhaps the use of the word "preference" might have softened it, but I think it was articulated between the parties that this is how it would go. However if I can get a sense of things, I will try to render some assistance in this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We would like to convey our position, too, should any changes in the timetable be made. We are certainly in favour of saving on time and expenses, but we also have to bear in mind the quality of the Defence. So we would like to remind Your Honours of the fact that Mr. Zigic's case is quite specific in many respects because it abounds in a large number of incidents; and in terms of incidents, we belong more to the Keraterm case, Sikovica, Kolundjia, and others. So we have to prepare for all three camps, Omarska, Keraterm, and Turnoplje, which is not the case for the other Defence counsel. Mr. Zigic had two indictments against him, and I think that we need a lot, a lot of time for preparation. We have managed to do quite a bit, in spite of changes in the Defence team. However, any changes in the order would cause a great deal of difficulty, and in that case we would not be able to meet the requirements of the Defence if the order were to be changed, or rather, if the proceedings are speeded up, because after all, Zigic is the only one who is being charged with very specific facts, in addition to Mr. Radic, and there are many such facts; and therefore, we have to prepare a great deal of Defence evidence. And also, our witnesses have to comment on a wide range of facts, so I appeal to the Chamber for their understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you very much Mr. Stojanovic. We will bear that in mind and take it into consideration and try to establish a timetable that will be as flexible as possible, and perhaps the way of doing it is - and I'm going to ask the legal officer of the Chamber, Mr. Fourmy - to contact each Defence counsel to see what the specifics of each Defence case are and establish a timetable so as to be able to respect it. But as you know, a timetable is an instrument that can always be changed. We have seen that in our cases. We had a timetable, and then suddenly it's gone because something occurs, so that is why we need to be flexible. But also, of course, we need to have an instrument of work in the form of timetable; otherwise, it's impossible to work. So we're now going to have a half-hour break, after which we'll come back for a private session to address the matters that we need to address in private.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. We shall move into private session to discuss the issues that we have for our private session, and then we'll go back into open session to take up the other matters that are pending. So may we move into private session now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.12 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. As you can see, Judge Fouad Riad is not with us. He had other obligations in another case, and therefore as we are at a Status Conference and we don't have to take any substantial decisions, we can continue. The questions that we still have to address is perhaps the question of opening statements, that is, Rule 84, and I think that there's a suggestion for the week beginning the 29th, I think it is, from the 29th to the 2nd of February. So regarding opening statements and Rule 84, I have the following question for you: We have not explicitly addressed the question when each Defence counsel is going to make his opening statement. I think, and as I have said, we haven't spoken about it explicitly, but I think that what we have said may lead us to believe that the opening statements will be made before the presentation of evidence by each accused. Nevertheless, I think there are certain aspects which may lead us to make opening statements at the same time, that is, the prosecution is the prosecution of five accused. There are five accused, and from the standpoint of the cross-examination by the Prosecution, it may be convenient to have the view of all Defence counsel, and we have the opportunity to do so without upsetting the organisation of work because if I am right, I think Mr. Krstan Simic needs three-quarters of an hour, I think, so that would make at least eight hours, which means we would need at least two days for the opening statements. So we could do that because we have at our disposal the Friday, and therefore all the witnesses that Mr. Krstan Simic has planned for this week could be heard during the week. So I think there are certain advantages to be gained by having the opening statements at the same time, but I also think that perhaps the Defence counsel may be taken by surprise. So I should like to hear the Defence counsel and the Prosecutor on this possibility, that is, opening statements at the same time which would begin on Monday, yes or no. Not at the same time, but one after another. Mr. Krstan Simic, I should have perhaps told you this before the break so you could discuss it amongst yourselves, but in any event, I give the floor to Mr. Krstan Simic now. For you it's the same thing; it doesn't affect you.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm beginning anyway on Monday; therefore, that doesn't affect me at all, so perhaps my colleagues should be heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you're quite right in saying that you would surprise us by this suggestion. When we discussed these opening statements, the position of all Defence counsel was that the opening statements should be made at the beginning of each respective case, and that is how we have prepared ourselves. That is all I am able to say. If you are asking this Defence team for its opinion, it would be for our opening statement to be made at the beginning of our case. Let me just add, as advised by my colleagues, that that was the case in the Celebici case, in the Foca case, and based on that, we took such a position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Nikolic. Mr. Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I concur with what Mr. Nikolic has just said. It is a position that we took earlier on, and we should like to abide by it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Jovanovic. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, our opinion is also very similar to the previous speakers. In my conviction, most of the opening statement should have to do with the points we intend to prove and the evidence we intend to present. We are still in the preparatory stages; therefore, an opening statement would be far too early for us to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Mr. Jovan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, our position is identical with that of other Defence counsel. We too are pressed by time, so we would like to make our opening statement before we begin our Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. For the record, Ms. Somers, only. I think we already are clear as to what the view is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We believe this material is entirely in your hands. Just our observation that normally the opening statement would respond to the Prosecution's case, which has essentially come. So thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So let's forget this idea. So each Defence counsel will make his opening statement prior to the presentation of evidence for the Defence. Another question of a practical nature is to see whether we can do anything in the week beginning the 29th of January through to the 2nd of February. The Chamber was informed that Ms. Somers has a suggestion, so perhaps we should hear Ms. Susan Somers' suggestion and then hear the reaction of Defence counsel. Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, we had had an opportunity to discuss trying to help out in some way with this week that should not be wasted, and although I admit it would be -- it would put us straining our resources, we would be willing, if the Court were so minded, to break up our cross of accused Kvocka, under the following conditions: that we would be prepared, after the first seven witnesses, to examine Kvocka on matters that arose during the course of or relate to the testimony of those seven witnesses, and then, when the case continues, we come back and complete our cross-examination on everything else that comes in and the case. We think this is the only real solution we could propose, and although it would strain us, we would be very willing to try to assist the Chamber in making the best use of that week. We would simply ask -- it is perhaps a creative solution and might need some guidance. And I have not talked -- I have not raised it with my learned opponents. I wanted first to see if the idea were even viable. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we have this suggestion. Thank you very much for it, Ms. Susan Somers, for trying to find a solution. We will see what the response of Defence counsel is in relation to this suggestion. Mr. Krstan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we would not be able to accept this suggestion, because really we cannot allow the accused to be cross-examined in different stages. We are ready to have his cross-examination completed at the end of the week. We see no grounds for cross-examining the accused after each witness. I think that we made a concession by allowing him to be cross-examined before all the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Krstan Simic. Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we are ready for the cross-examination of Mr. Radic, but that it should be completed in that week. So our position is the same as Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for your cooperation. So I think we are in a position when we will have to waste that week. I must share with the parties some concerns that the Chamber has at this moment. The point is that we have to complete this case before July, or around July, certainly before the summer holidays. I think there's no need to elaborate on the reasons. You understand them. If I tell you that the mandate of the Judges ends in November, I think you will immediately understand what I mean. I don't have to go into any further explanations. In other words, it is absolutely necessary to complete the case. So therefore, we absolutely have to make the best of all the time we have available to us. Perhaps we will allow this opportunity to pass, but we cannot, we cannot accept any further waste of time. It is not truly a waste of time, as you know, because it hadn't been programmed in advance, but the Chamber has other cases, has other obligations as well which need to be carried out at the same time. Regarding this question of timetable, I told you that I would ask Monsieur Olivier Fourmy to contact each Defence counsel and the Prosecutor to agree on a timetable that will serve our objectives and that will also reflect your requirements, and after that perhaps we will have a final timetable. Something else that I need to tell you is that the Chamber is not in a position now to fix definitely a timetable with you, because we still don't have definitive information as to when the other case would resume, which means that the Chamber will probably be able to do so in about two weeks' time. Therefore, now we're going to work for five weeks in continuity, and perhaps we will try to meet the requests for pauses. We will see. But after that there will be a pause. So we're going to work five weeks consecutively, in succession, so let me look at the calendar. So we're going to work the week beginning the 22nd, which is Monday, means through to Friday. That is not the case this week as there was an error made regarding the 26th when we will not be sitting. Then we'll be sitting from the 5th till the 9th, from the 12th to the 16th, from the 19th to the 23rd, from the 26th of February to the 2nd of March. No, I'm sorry. The 26th until the 2nd of March, that is when the break will be. So when I was saying five weeks, I had included the 29th to the 2nd, but no. So we'll not be sitting from the 29th to the 2nd of February because we haven't found a solution for that. Then the 26th until the 2nd of March, that will be a free week. So we still don't know whether we will resume this case on the 6th because the 5th is a holiday, so we'll be working from the 6th to the 9th. We don't know whether we will be resuming this case then or the other case, and it is for that reason that I was saying that we cannot fix at this stage a definitive timetable, but we will do our best to respect the dates set earlier on, bearing in mind the possibility -- bearing in mind the fact that certain programming has been made, and if we are not able to respect them, we will have to change them. But we will do our best to respect the earlier programming made. I'm sorry, I've been given a note here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what we can say for certain is that we will begin on Monday with the Defence case for Mr. Kvocka. We will have an opening statement, and after that, the testimony of witnesses. In any event, as Friday is free, if we haven't finished with the witnesses, we can use that Friday. So when I say that we're not working on the 26th, we won't be working if we don't need it, if we finish with all the witnesses on Thursday. If we need Friday, we will use the day. Mr. Krstan Simic, is that okay, then?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I have been informed that all the witnesses are ready to come here, and I hope that they will have no problem boarding the plane.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have the parties any other questions to raise before we adjourn? Yes, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
