utterances.text: The only observation we would make regarding the timetable is, as we have that -- the three solid weeks in February, that would give the Kvocka case a total of four weeks. Now, if they were to end somewhere in that four weeks, we would be requesting, as you suggested, Your Honour, a short break there. If in fact we're in the last week of that schedule, the 19th to the 23rd, that may be the point where Kvocka ends and Kos's schedule begins, so we would ask for your indulgence and flexibility when we see when Kvocka is likely to end and Kos will begin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. O'Sullivan, excuse me, but as I have said for the reasons I have told you about, we're trying to make the best of the time. Do you have any urgent need for this pause? Couldn't that be dealt with in some other way?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, the whole, the whole question of the timing will hinge on how long the Kvocka case takes, and I think that may include how much cross-examination the Prosecution may request or need of affidavits, whether we do videolink. There is some uncertainty in just how long the whole Kvocka case will take, and we'll see that as we move through the month of February. But that's all we'd like to flag at this point, is to state our position on our need for some lead time before we make the transition to our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: What do you consider, in the abstract, I know, but what do you consider a sufficient pause?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Let me first say we would not want to find ourselves finishing Kvocka on a Wednesday and thinking we could start on Thursday, the following day. If it's mid-week like that, three, four, five days is what we would look for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: How about if it's a Friday?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Friday/Monday is pretty tight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Friday/Tuesday is all right?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I'm just exploring what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I think which days off are relevant here, whether it's the weekend or mid-week. We can probably gauge this later as we move through the Kvocka case, but I think you can see our concern, that we'd like to be in a position to have our people ready to come and be here and we could begin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps to follow-up on this question raised by the Kos Defence, perhaps I could ask Mr. Krstan Simic whether you can give us an idea now already of your own schedule, if I may put it that way. What is your timetable now?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have 26 witnesses. Twenty-three of them will certainly appear in Court if time allows, of course. We have affidavits, we have the cross-examination, and finally, we have the cross-examination of Mr. Kvocka. Ms. Somers has said it will take a day or two. I would be very glad and happy if I can complete everything by the 16th of February. That would be a few days more than the others, but I'm not sure that I will succeed. I would be very happy to complete the presentation of my case on the 16th of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So perhaps -- I don't think we can make a final assessment today because we still don't know what will be the response of the Prosecutor regarding affidavits that you have received, if I understood things well. Thank you, Mr. Krstan Simic. Maybe we can come back to you. Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just wanted to clarify a point that Mr. Simic attempted to represent. Our comment about length of cross was minimally a day or two, minimally. And this would lead into another question, because I understand that the cross of -- that the direct went on for up to four days? Four days. And we would, of course, have to reserve, as it were, equal time. We'll try to be as crisp as possible. But one question that would arise - and I hope this is not an inappropriate time to raise it, but it will help us plan a bit - is if there is a rule which prevails in this Chamber about the duration of cross and the duration of -- the relationship of the length of cross to the length of direct, when Radic testified, he effectively adopted something like to two days' worth of Kvocka's testimony. We will nonetheless have to deal with the issues with respect to Radic, and therefore just to let the Chamber know that when we factor in the time needed for crossing Radic, it will not be based on that quick adoption of number of days' worth of testimony, but we will have to go into the testimony that was the subject of that number of days. And again, I wanted to let the Chamber know in advance, having looked at how things transpired, that that would be a factor in overall time assessment. If we move on to anything else, I just wanted to return, when the Chamber is prepared to allow me to, to a quick couple of points on R, which we discussed just before the break, but whenever the Chamber is ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Excuse me one second. I just want to --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I think we're safe. It appears to have been open session, so there's no issue. I wanted to bring to the attention of the Chamber that I did review again the testimony during the lunch break, and I will only amplify my comment to say that although [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: [redacted] Secondly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. We're in open session now. We are not in private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: My understanding, Your Honour, was that it was open session, this testimony. The transcript I'm looking at says, "Witness R, open session," so I -- yes. Have I misunderstood the status of the session? My understanding is that it was all open. Okay. Thank you. Secondly, perhaps more importantly, is our concern about the invocation by the Defence now on statements. First of all, the discussion opened this morning with the idea -- with a concern over the use of 94 ter, the deceased 94 ter, as it were, for the new 92 bis, and it was -- it appeared that the Defence was unified in its desire to proceed under 94 ter generally. In other words, 92 bis was not going to be, for preparation purposes, necessarily governing. To even suggest the transcript at this point, whether use of a transcript, which would be coming in presumably under 92 bis, appears to us to be a bit of a selective use of 94 and a selective use of 92, which I think would very much disadvantage us. Secondly, if in fact the Chamber were looking at the appropriateness under 92, should it consider it, the language of it - and again, it is a very untested provision; in fact, it is, as Judge Wald pointed out, effective as of today - does not contemplate the use of transcript evidence where the issue goes to the guilt of the accused. And I would just call that to the Chamber's attention, because I think under no set of circumstances would we feel that it were even-handed to allow a transcript now when in fact we also would not benefit -- or we did not benefit from the change in the Rule. And we were, in fact, based on I think the 4th of July decision of 2000, it was indicated that we could not use the prior transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: The only thing I want to add to your thing is that my understanding that -- leave out for a moment new 92 bis and however it comes to be interpreted, but under the prior jurisprudence we had not only - the prior or the one we started out with here - we not only had 94 ter affidavit evidence, but you did have some jurisprudence in the Tribunal apart from 94 ter that allowed transcripts in certain situations, like Blaskic and Aleksovski, that was, in certain circumstances, at least, upheld by the appellate. So it wasn't a question of everything having to be -- to go by way of 94 ter. That's all I --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, and in fact transcripts had been used widely in other Chambers, but this Chamber did not permit it for the Prosecution, and so we would ask that essentially there be no shift in policy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see Mr. O'Sullivan on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes. May I respond to that, Your Honour? This issue is relevant to our defence, and in my submission, on July 4th of last year, Your Honours did in fact rule that transcripts are admissible, and that was in keeping with the Aleksovski decision, which, as Your Honours know, is an appellate decision which is binding on this Chamber. The Prosecution has pointed out in their response to 65 ter that they were not allowed to submit the transcript from the Tadic case of Witness A, and that was quite correct. Witness A testified. Your Honours did not allow them to submit in addition Witness A's transcript from Tadic because the witness was here. The Aleksovski situation is when the witness is not coming to testify, and if a party brings the transcript within the parameters of the Aleksovski appeals ruling, it's admissible. That's been the findings of this Tribunal since Aleksovski, in Kordic, and I think Your Honours know better than I what -- your recent decision in Tuta and Stela regarding the admissibility of transcripts from other proceedings which can be brought within the Aleksovski rule. I can tell Your Honours that it is our intention for Kos to rely on that decision and that ruling. Now, clearly the language of 92 bis seems to, on the face of it, change the Aleksovski rule or place certain limitations on the Aleksovski rule. When the time comes, we'll make our submissions on what we think is appropriate, given Rule 60, and what we say is exculpatory evidence from transcripts in other trials, but for now I just wanted to make that point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. O'Sullivan, for drawing our attention to this. I was just about to pose the question myself. I would not like to take a position regarding the decision of the Chamber, but it is true, I think, that we made a distinction. If we place this whole issue of transcript within the overall discussion that we had, on a number of occasions, not just once, but repeatedly in this case, we have in a sense compared transcripts to when we have the witness here, to the opening -- to the preliminary statements. It is true what Mr. O'Sullivan has said, for witnesses who were present. But for others, the question that we discussed, as far as I can remember, was to tender into the record transcript automatically or after a discussion, because we proceeded from the principle that transcripts are public and therefore they can be used in the case. And the position that we took at the time was: Yes, they are public, but to be admitted into evidence it is necessary to discuss the matter within this case, and that is I think the position that we took. So it is true that we took a position regarding prior statements, and we include there not only the statements given to the Prosecutor but also the statements given to administrative authorities by the witness, for instance, the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And as there was a disagreement there, we agreed that the counsel could use the statements here for their cross-examination, but those documents were never tendered or admitted. So you will remember that there were counsel who wanted to tender into evidence only the part used, and the other party said, "No. No. The entire document needs to be tendered." The other party said, "No, because then we will be admitting into evidence information on which I had no opportunity to cross-examine." And so we rendered the decision that the parties may use either transcripts from hearings or prior statements given to the Prosecutor or any other statements given to the authorities, but not to admit them when the witness is here in the courtroom. However, we have an entirely different situation when the witness is not here, and I think that we decided that. But we can check. I think Mr. O'Sullivan is right when he says what he says. That is my impression. As I said, I was saying this without committing myself to a ruling of the Chamber. So I think we will take that into consideration. The Chamber will decide. We said that we would take a decision today, but you must understand that there are questions that require more in-depth consideration, and therefore we will try to render our ruling Monday morning. We will come back with our decision. I see that Mr. Stojanovic wanted to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I should like to thank my learned friend O'Sullivan, because that was our opinion too. There obviously appears to be a misunderstanding with Ms. Somers. She said that one of these names - I don't know whether I may say it in public now - that one of these names is not mentioned. [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [redacted]. So we have three persons for which Zigic has been accused and about which there are very detailed explanations in this transcript, very detailed and clear. In any event, it is our submission that this is a document whose authenticity cannot be contested in any way and which, in our opinion, has far greater weight than many other documents that have been admitted by the Tribunal from other sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can I try just to be of assistance to the Chamber in giving some locations of testimony, if it will help. The reference for the July 4th conference is, in the unofficial, not corrected version, page 3522, if it would be of assistance, and 23; and then in the Tadic matter it's referring to page 2325, et seq., and particularly 2338. The date would have been 17 July 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I think we've come to the end. We'll take care of this, all this, and then -- excuse me. Mr. Krstan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know whether this is a question for the Chamber, but we're beginning on Monday, and tomorrow is a non-working day. Could the registry allow me to come with the witnesses, to come to the court to brief them a little bit so that they shouldn't be in any way surprised once they come to the courtroom? And I think this has been a practice applied by the Prosecution regularly. So can I bring my witnesses to the Tribunal tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krstan Simic, do you cooperate with the Witness and Victims Unit, or do you do all that by yourself?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do cooperate with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, would this be a problem, the request made by Mr. Krstan Simic, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: If he would give me a brief minute to discuss this with my superiors, I'll be able to confirm, because this is new for me. I've never had this request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krstan Simic, I think the best thing to do would be as follows: Madam Registrar will do everything she can for you to be able to do so on Monday, so we'll begin the hearing at 10.00. I'm saying this because it's important. We'll begin the hearing at 10.00. Is that all right? 10.00. And in the meantime, Madam Registrar, you will take all the necessary measures. Something else that I should like to say. Could you tell us, Madam Registrar, whether you have regulated the question of the numbers for the exhibits?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I have met with the Defence counsel and we discussed -- and they're in agreement with how we will handle the protected witnesses and exhibits, so that has been taken care of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I think finally we have indeed come to the end this conference. Thank you for your cooperation. We'll be back here on Monday to begin -- or rather, to finish as soon as possible. As I have told you, when there are questions that take time, we will discuss those questions in the afternoon, but we will devote the morning hearings to the witnesses. So perhaps we may need to have several Status Conferences to address the question of the rhythm of work. We will bear in mind what the Kos defence has requested, having a pause if possible, but we will have to deal with that as we go along. So for today, all that remains for me to do is to wish you a good weekend, success in your work, and we will meet again on Monday at 10.00. Do not forget, 10.00 Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: be reconvened on Monday, the 22nd day of January, 2001, at 10.00 a.m.
